bio.en: Hamilton Helmer is a strategy legend and the author of 7 Powers, the widely praised framework for identifying and building sustainable competitive advantage ('moats'), credited by leaders like Peter Thiel and Reed Hastings for helping them build durable companies.
bio.zh: Hamilton Helmer 是战略领域的传奇人物，也是《七种力量》（7 Powers）的作者；这本书提出了识别与构建可持续竞争优势（“护城河”）的广为推崇的框架，被 Peter Thiel、Reed Hastings 等领导者誉为帮助他们打造持久公司的关键。

summary.en: Hamilton explains that real 'power' requires both a benefit and a barrier—speed or a great team alone is a treadmill, not a moat—and walks through how startups can begin developing sources of power early. He covers which powers companies mistakenly think they have, how power relates to strategy and moats, and what individual PMs (not just leaders) can do with these insights. The conversation also explores how AI is reshaping both market entry and the classic sources of power, plus a preview of his next book.
summary.zh: Hamilton 解释说，真正的“力量”需要同时具备收益与壁垒——光有速度或优秀团队只是 treadmill（跑步机），而非护城河，并讲解了初创公司如何尽早开始培育力量来源。他谈到了公司常误以为自己拥有、实则没有的力量，力量如何与战略和护城河关联，以及普通 PM（不只是领导者）能如何利用这些洞见。对话还探讨了 AI 如何重塑市场进入方式与经典力量来源，并预告了他的下一本书。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in a lot of decks it's like, "Oh, we have the most amazing team. We move the fastest." You mention how rarely is that actually a power?
turns.zh: 很多商业方案都是这样：“我们拥有最出色的团队，行动最迅速。” 但你会发现，这种所谓的“权力”实际上多半是空谈。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: You're on a treadmill and if you stop running on that treadmill, you get creamed, but it's not power. The things that drive operational excellence can be mimicked.
turns.zh: 你就像在跑步机上奔跑，只要停下来，就会被淘汰，但这并非真正的权力。那些推动卓越运营的因素是可以被模仿的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually talk about achieving these powers.
turns.zh: 让我们实际探讨如何获取这些权力。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: There's a thing called power progression. There are times when certain types of power are available. The path to power is where the rubber meets the road.
turns.zh: 存在一种叫做“权力进化”的概念。某些类型的权力在特定时期会出现。通往权力的道路才是真正考验人的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's even more my pleasure. I want to start by talking about when power becomes important. turns.zh: 更荣幸了。首先，我想谈谈权力何时变得重要。您建议创始人在何时开始从产品市场契合度前期和后期角度思考权力问题？早期花时间思考权力是否值得？显然，适当思考固然有益，但在找到真正受用户青睐的产品之前，创始人应当以何种程度和严肃性来关注权力问题？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: One of the things that has really surprised me in the last five years has been that my understanding of the answer to that question has changed. And before I thought it was you do product market fit and then you do strategy, and if you try and put strategy before product market fit, it is not much you can do with it. That's wrong. Actually, I mentioned before one of the great pleasures for me in my work is being able to talk to company founders and one of the things that has surprised me is that conversations with them, even at an early stage about strategic matters have a richness and relevance to me that was unexpected. (00:05:41): And founders are practical people. I mean it's very hard to do what they're doing and they have to be extremely focused and choose what's worthwhile spending time on. And so in observing their reactions and that dialogue, I could see that there was something going on that was meaningful to them. And this second book we're working on, we'll tease out why that's so more, but the answer to your question is when should you thinking about this? The answer is always. And that's an odd answer. And so even before you have product-market fit, it's worth thinking about strategy. Now it's not strategy in the sense of this fully articulated strategic planning, we're going to do this, these are going to be the competitors, this is how we're going to answer them. This is how we'll price. Not like that at all. At the earlier stage, you can imagine wildly more degrees of freedom and the questions are of the business propositions that you're thinking of in trying to get to product-market fit, what are the underlying characteristics that might tilt them towards the availability of power or not? (00:07:10): And those actually are meaningful conversations and certainly by no means certain. You're tilting probabilities, you're not creating a determinative things. And then later on, once you've already have product-market fit, then you have to understand your source of power to understand what competitive position is because then you have to establish that. And then later on in a more stable phase when you're in a stability phase of business, you have to know what your source of power is if you have one, because you have to know how to defend it. And then also it is also the foundational knowledge that you need for if there's another step. Because another thing that's quite surprising about iconic businesses is they often have a second act or a third act or fourth act. I mean think of AWS or Intel going into CPUs or Apple going into iPhones, all not the origin of business. And that's actually common, not unusual, and that's starting the process all over again.
turns.zh: 过去五年中最令我惊讶的一点是，我对这个问题的理解发生了变化。此前我认为是先完成产品市场契合度，再制定战略，而若试图将战略置于产品市场契合度之前，往往收效甚微。这种观点是错误的。事实上，我之前曾提到，在与创业者交流时，早期阶段就围绕战略问题展开的对话，其深度和相关性远超我的预期。（00:05:41）创业者都是务实之士。他们所做之事本就极具挑战性，必须高度专注，明智取舍。因此，通过观察他们的反应和对话，我发现其中蕴含着对他们意义非凡的思考要点。我们正在撰写的第二本书将深入剖析其中的深层原因，但关于何时该思考战略的问题，答案是：永远不嫌早。这或许听起来有些奇怪。即便在尚未实现产品市场契合度之际，战略思考同样重要。这里所说的战略并非指那种精心策划的完整规划——比如确定竞争对手、制定应对策略、设定定价策略等——而是更具探索性的阶段。在早期阶段，您可以畅想更广泛的可能性空间，围绕实现产品市场契合度的商业模式思考深层问题：哪些潜在特质会影响获取权力的可能性？（00:07:10）这些对话意义非凡，但结论绝非确定性结论。您只是在调整概率权衡，而非锁定定局。随后，在产品市场契合度实现后，您必须理解自身权力来源，以明确竞争定位；再往后，当业务进入稳定期，更要明确权力来源——这是捍卫竞争优势的基石。更重要的是，这也是下一步探索的基础认知。标志性企业的惊人之处在于，他们往往会开启第二幕、第三幕甚至第四幕。以AWS、英特尔向CPU领域转型、苹果进军iPhone市场为例，这些都非原生业务。这种现象极为常见，绝非特例，这意味着每一次成功都意味着全新的探索之旅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You mentioned this word strategy. I want to set a little foundation here. How does strategy relate to power when people are thinking about these two concepts? And then do you have just a nice definition of what strategy is? Everyone's always just like, "What the heck do you mean when you're talking about the strategy?"
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到了这个战略概念。我想先打个基础。当人们思考战略和权力这两个概念时，战略与权力有何关联？你能否给出一个简洁的战略定义？人们总是会问：“你说战略是什么意思啊？”

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: As I said, I'm a concept person and so when you develop concepts, you have to be very highly constrained by their usefulness. I'm a great fan of the great mathematician, John von Neumann, and he had a view which really irritated a lot of mathematicians, which is that if mathematics wasn't guided by what was useful, it would become, I think the word he used was aesthetic to aesthetic. And so any concept developments like that, it needs to be guided by usefulness. And so in dealing with strategy, the question is what domain of things do you want to include in that conversation? Because the term is ubiquitous in business. I mean do a Google search sometime. I've done one recently on Google Scholar for the word strategy and you'll get a million, I'm not exaggerating, a million hits. And so strategy for some people might mean everything that gets to the pile, it gets to the top of a pile in terms of what you have to do that year. (00:09:58): Everything is... And that's a perfectly legitimate definition, but what I have found is that there is a very important narrowing that makes it much more useful. So that's coming back to what I was saying [inaudible 00:10:17] makes it much more useful to the business. So my view is that you want to focus, it's very useful for a business to focus on the fundamental determinants of business value and that's an arbitrary choice. It could be something else, but I can tell you from decades of business experience that that narrowing is very useful. And then so once you make that... Once you reach that understanding, it tells you some important things. So if you understand what drives business value, I mean if you do the math of it right, it's NPV of cash flow, right? Expected cash flow. And what that tells you is that strategy is a long time concept. You're looking far out in the future. (00:11:10): So think of Pearl Harbor, Pearl Harbor for the Japanese was this enormous tactical success. They just destroyed the US ability, naval ability in the Pacific Ocean and the worst possible strategic move because it completely solved Franklin Delano Roosevelt's problem of how he could get the US citizens on board to attacking Hitler. The strategy of it was US's industrial might would eventually win the war and population. And the difference there is time constant, tactical short, strategy long. And so if you focus on value that narrows what you think about and allows you to get rather concise and offer up advice to founders about what they need to pay attention to.
turns.zh: 正如我所说，我是个概念主义者，所以在开发概念时，必须高度关注其实用性。我非常崇拜伟大数学家约翰·冯·诺伊曼。他有一个观点，让许多数学家感到不满——他认为，如果数学不以实用性为导向，就会变得，嗯，他用词是“美学化”的。因此，任何概念的发展都必须以实用性为导向。谈到战略，关键问题在于你想将哪些领域纳入讨论范畴？因为“战略”一词在商业中无处不在。随便用谷歌搜索一下。我最近在谷歌学术上搜索了“战略”这个词，得到的结果不下百万条，我没夸大其词，真的有百万条。所以对某些人来说，战略可能意味着一切需要优先处理的事务。（00:09:58）一切都是……这是一个完全合理的定义，但我发现，通过一个重要的缩减范围，可以让它对商业更有用。回到我之前说的，[听不清 00:10:17]这样做对商业更有用。所以我的观点是，企业应该专注于商业价值的基本决定因素，这是一个任意选择的范畴。也可以是其他东西，但根据我几十年的商业经验，这种缩减范围非常有用。一旦你理解了这一点，就会得到一些重要启示。比如，如果你理解什么驱动着商业价值，正确计算的话，就是现金流的净现值，对吧？预期现金流。这告诉你，战略是一个长期概念。你要着眼于未来。（00:11:10）想想珍珠港事件。对日本人来说，珍珠港是巨大的战术胜利。他们彻底摧毁了美国在太平洋地区的海军力量。但这却是最糟糕的战略决策，因为它彻底解决了富兰克林·德拉诺·罗斯福让美国公民支持对希特勒发动攻击的难题。美国的工业实力最终会赢得战争，加上人口优势。这里的时间维度是战术短，战略长。所以如果你专注于价值，就会缩小思考范围，更能为创业者提供简洁的建议，告诉他们需要关注什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So then how specifically is power informing strategies? Like the way you think about it, focus on your power and that will inform your strategy?
turns.zh: 那么权力具体如何影响战略？比如你思考这个问题时，专注于自己的权力，这会影响你的战略吗？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Earlier I talked about these economic structures that provide durability of return in terms of refuge from withering arbitrage of everybody who wants to eat your lunch. And so that's what power is. So you have to understand what is an economics? You're asking me questions that get pretty deep into theory or I hope you don't, this is too conceptual. But you have to say, you have to understand how competition takes place and say what is it that creates some kind of refuge? And what it is is there's something in what you do that gives you either a cost or price advantage over others. So let's say you're lower cost and that's the benefit. And the barrier side is that there's something that is durable about that that makes it over time that you can't, the competitors can't take away from you. So benefit and a barrier, we call it the to be or not to be test. And if you have that, you can think of that immediately translating into a value because that will give you good margins out into the foreseeable future, which is what you're after. (00:13:44): I don't know if that's... We're getting into the weeds here, but that's what it's about. And so power is those structures. Let me give you a quick example. So one I use in the book. So Netflix with scale economies, they have more subscribers. The cost of their content is a very large fixed cost, about 50% of their cost structure every year. They can take that fixed cost and spread it over more subscribers so their cost per subscriber is less versus somebody with fewer subscribers. So if they face the same prices for subscriptions as their competitors, they will be more profitable. And that's a scale economy and that's an example of a type of power and a common one I'd say. But these things are hard to achieve, right? Because there's the holy grail.
turns.zh: 早些时候，我谈到了这些经济结构，它们能在面对所有想分食你利润的竞争时，提供回报的持久性。这就是权力的本质。所以你必须理解什么是经济学？你问的问题太深入理论层面了，希望你别这样，这太概念化了。但你得明白，竞争是如何发生的，以及是什么创造了某种庇护所？答案在于，你所做的事情能为你带来成本或价格优势，胜过其他人。比如说，你的成本更低，这就是优势。而障碍在于，这种优势具有持久性，随着时间推移，竞争对手无法从你这里夺走它。所以优势和障碍，我们称之为生死抉择测试。如果你具备这些，你就能立即将其转化为价值，因为这将在可预见的未来为你带来良好的利润回报，这正是你所追求的。（00:13:44）：我不知道这是否...我们在这里钻牛角尖了，但这就是关键所在。所以权力就是这些结构。我给你们举个快速例子。书中提到的Netflix凭借规模经济，拥有更多订阅用户。他们的内容成本是固定成本很高的支出，每年占成本结构的50%左右。他们可以将这笔固定成本分摊到更多订阅用户上，所以每个订阅用户的成本比订阅用户较少的公司更低。因此，如果他们与竞争对手收取相同的订阅价格，他们就会更有利可图。这就是规模经济，也是权力的一种例子，我觉得这是很常见的一种。但这些东西很难实现，对吧？因为这就是圣杯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's actually talk about achieving these powers. Essentially the argument here is your power informs everything you do because this is the thing that'll allow you to stay durable and competitive and last. There's seven powers. We're not going to talk about all of them. If you want to go understand each of them, go read the book.
turns.zh: 那我们实际上来谈谈如何获得这些权力。本质上，我们的论点是，你的权力决定了你所做的一切，因为这能让你保持持久、竞争力和生命力。有七种权力，我们不会一一讨论。如果你想了解每一种，就去读那本书吧。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah. Let's not. That conversation always goes too long.
turns.zh: 是啊，还是别讨论了。那样的讨论总是太冗长了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So what I'm wondering is, okay, so say you're looking at this list of seven powers and you're a specific type of startup, do you have a heuristic that tells you here's most likely the power and set of subsets that will most likely be an option for you? Like B2B SaaS companies, is there a smaller subset? Probably one of these has to be one of your options versus B2C.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。所以我想知道的是，好吧，如果你看看这七种权力的列表，而你是一家特定类型的初创公司，你有没有一个启发式方法，能告诉你最有可能的权力和子集会成为你的选择？比如B2B SaaS公司，有没有一个更小的子集？可能其中之一必须是你的选择之一，而非B2C。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: That's a great question Lenny, because I think the path to power is where the rubber meets the road and it's very complicated and nuanced. But I'll give you a few thoughts along it and frankly our next book, the Second Invention, that's what it's about. It's about power, the entire book.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的问题，Lenny，因为我认为通往权力的道路是关键所在，它非常复杂和微妙。但我会就此给出一些想法，坦白说，我们的下一本书《第二次发明》就是关于这个的。整本书都是关于权力的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [Inaudible 00:15:56] I'll try to read it.
turns.zh: [00:15:56不可听清]我试试看读一下。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: So in a book there's a thing called power progression, which says there are... It tells over the cycle of a business, there are times when certain types of power are available and the converse of that is times when they're not available. And so there's some that only are really available in when you reach a stability phase of a business pretty far out there. (00:16:25): And so if you're starting a company, take those off the table. So those two are branding and process power. So often I find that there's a confusion about this because brand recognition for a startup may be incredibly important, but you can get brand recognition by buying an ad in the Super Bowl. That's not power, that you paid for it. So take branding and process power and process power is really operational excellence on steroids and usually is imitable, so it's usually not. (00:17:05): So take those off the table and then a resource type of power, which is you have something that is of value that if you transferred it to somebody else it would be of value to them, but you own the rights. So the barrier is law for example, or lack of knowledge from others. And there are classes of businesses that are like that. So prescription pharmaceuticals, if you are the first person to come up with Viagra, that's worth a lot of money. If you took that license and gave it to somebody else, it'd be worth a lot of money to them. But that's a different class and it's usually not the types of things that I'm dealing with and it's obvious to everybody. So the key challenge there is can you invent a pharmaceutical that's effective for a large market. So you can take those three off the table and that then leaves counter positioning, scale economies, switching costs and network economies. (00:18:13): And the important thing to keep in mind there is that they're sequenced. So almost every startup that you want to deal with starts with counter positioning because remember what product market fit is primarily is a substitution. You are coming up with a way to satisfy a more or less existing need in a novel way that creates more value. Now sometimes you tap into entirely new needs, but it's not so often. I mean Amazon was up against brick and mortar stores, Google was up against Yahoo and so on, and so you're usually substituting and that substitution, so your competition at that point is functional competition. (00:19:19): And if you don't have counter positioning at that point you're pretty high risk from an incumbent who already has the capabilities necessary to do that. They just have to extend their product or do this or that, but counter positioning is the refuge from that. And then you go into the other three types of power scale economies, switching costs and network economies, and those depend on your scale relative to competitors. This is pretty cursory, but that's what I'd say. I'll focus on those four and I would recommend that you think pretty hard about whether you think you have counter positioning to start.
turns.zh: 书中有一个叫做“权力递进”的概念，它指出在企业的生命周期中，有些类型的权力在特定时期可用，而另一些则在特定时期不可用。比如，在企业达到稳定阶段后，品牌和流程权力才会真正显现。（00:16:25）所以如果你正在创办公司，这些因素可以先排除。品牌和流程权力通常会让人混淆，因为初创企业的品牌认知固然重要，但你花钱买超级碗广告也能获得品牌知名度——那不是真正的权力，而是你为此付了钱。所以品牌和流程权力需要排除。流程权力本质上是卓越的运营能力，而且通常容易被模仿，所以通常不算。（00:17:05）再排除资源型权力——即你拥有某种有价值的东西，如果转让给别人，他们也能获益，但你拥有知识产权。比如处方药领域，如果你率先研发出伟哥，那价值巨大。若将授权给别人，他们也能赚大钱。但这类业务模式通常不适用于我所讨论的初创企业，而且大家都心知肚明。关键挑战在于能否发明出面向大市场的有效药物。（00:18:13）需要注意的是，权力类型是按顺序出现的。几乎所有初创企业都会从反向定位入手，因为产品市场匹配本质上是替代性创新。你要以新奇方式满足现有需求，从而创造更多价值。有时能开拓全新需求，但这种情况并不常见。比如亚马逊挑战实体店，谷歌挑战雅虎等。所以你通常在进行替代性创新，此时竞争对手是功能性竞争。（00:19:19）若此时没有反向定位，初创企业将面临被现有企业压制的高风险。现有企业只需改进产品或采取相应策略即可，但反向定位是抵御这种威胁的屏障。接下来是规模经济、转换成本和网络经济，这些都取决于相较竞争对手的规模优势。这只是粗略概述，但以上就是我的观点。我会重点关注这四种权力，并建议大家认真思考自己是否具备反向定位的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I actually want to double down on that thread, but just to summarize, I have the list here. Basically you're saying if you're an early stage startup, the four to really that are actually potential powers for you at least early on, counter positioning, which your point is you could just start with that. That's essentially positioning and business model design, which happens at the beginning and then you can start to think about network economy, scale economy, switching costs as powers.
turns.zh: 太棒了。实际上我还想再深入探讨一下那个话题，但先总结一下。我这儿有份清单。基本上，如果你是一家初创公司，至少在早期阶段，以下四点可能是你的潜在优势：反向定位（你提到可以从这一点入手）。这本质上涉及定位和商业模式设计（这在初期就需要考虑），然后再去思考网络经济、规模经济和转换成本等优势。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Right. And you've done the right thing by not having me go through and define each of those. But your listeners will need to go back to my book and see what those things are to get... We're going through the shorthand as we should, but all of what we've said won't be completely obvious to them.
turns.zh: 好的。你没让我逐一解释这些术语，这很明智。但听众可能需要回看我的书才能理解这些概念。我们现在只是简要提一下，但这些内容对他们来说可能不太直观。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think a simple Google search I find just gives you a very simple definition of these.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得在谷歌上搜索一下就能找到这些术语的简单定义。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. There's some people who have done some really good summaries of this.
turns.zh: 没错。确实有一些人对此做了很好的总结。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or ChatGPT, even better in a lot of cases.
turns.zh: 或者用ChatGPT，在很多情况下效果更好。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: ChatGPT if they get it right sometimes I find they hallucinate.
turns.zh: 有时候ChatGPT如果理解错了，还会产生幻觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hallucinate an eighth power. You mentioned how some companies think they have a certain power or it's common to think you have a certain power. If you look at every startup deck, there's always like, "Here's our moat, here's the way we're going to have barriers to entry." I'm guessing in almost every case they're delusional about the power that they actually have and the power they think they'll have. Do you also find that to be true that often founders are wrong about how much barrier they've actually created and is there a power you often find most wrong and mistaken?
turns.zh: 比如幻想出第八种优势。你提到有些公司认为自己拥有某种优势，或者普遍认为自己拥有某种优势。看看每个初创公司的演示文稿，里面总是写着“我们的护城河在这里，我们将如何建立进入壁垒”。我猜几乎每个案例中，他们都高估了自己实际拥有的优势和预期将拥有的优势。你是否也发现，很多创始人对自己实际创造的壁垒程度存在误解？有没有某种优势是他们最常误判的？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, so I agree with your observation, but I don't want to be unkind. So I mean there are two things to keep in mind here in terms of making people feel better about that incorrect slide in the deck. One is that founders have to be optimistic. I think it's an important quality that they maybe understate the risk a little bit, but they're so committed to I'm going to do this thing that they go through that and that may give them an advantage over a large corporation trying to do the same thing. The other is that despite the name 7 Powers, which makes it sound like, oh, you can sort this out. Actually understanding whether or not there is a type of power in place is hard. I mean I did it with my colleagues here at Strategy Capital and we're looking at a well-known company, it might take us weeks to answer that question for a single company. (00:22:47): And it comes down to the hard part is industry economics is what really are the economic relationships and it's very hard. So with those caveats that... Give them some courtesy, I'll say some of the obvious ones are I mentioned before, people sometimes think they have branding power, but another one that I think I've heard you mention is people often think that they get scale economies through data. And I'd say that that's possible, but it's rare. And the reason it's rare is not because there aren't scale economies in data, but rather that the range of scale that the existing competitors have are often large enough to be able to put them in shouting distance of each so that the differences in their cost per unit is not that great. (00:23:50): The curve flattens in other words, which is typical of any, because the most common scale economy is you've got a big fixed cost and you prorate that. And as you get more and more scale, the percentage cost advantage of a fixed cost advantage like that goes down and that often. So that's a pretty frequent one that we see. We laugh whenever we hear somebody say they have a flywheel, which gives you the idea of network economies. There are often flywheels, the ones that really are material, are rare. The key thing here is materiality, not whether the flywheel exists, but whether the effect is strong enough to really tilt returns.
turns.zh: 是的，我同意你的观察，但我不想显得无礼。所以，在让人们对演示文稿中的错误幻灯片感觉好受些这件事上，我们需要注意两点：第一，创始人必须保持乐观。我认为这是一项重要的品质，他们或许会略微低估风险，但他们对“我要做成这件事”的执着，会让他们克服这些困难，从而比试图做同样事的大型企业更具优势。第二，尽管7 Powers这个名字听起来好像能解决问题，但实际上理解某种权力是否存在并非易事。比如，我和Strategy Capital的同事研究过一家知名公司，光是回答这个问题就花了好几周时间。（00:22:47）关键在于，行业经济学才是真正关键所在——即经济关系的本质，这非常复杂。所以在提出这些批评时，我得先说一些显而易见的观点，比如人们有时认为自己拥有品牌权力，但我记得你提过的一个观点是，人们常认为能通过数据获得规模经济。我认为这确实有可能，但概率很低。原因不在于数据不存在规模经济，而是现有竞争对手的规模通常大到足以让他们在单位成本上形成接近的竞争。因此，成本差异并不明显。（00:23:50）换句话说，曲线趋于平缓，这是任何行业的典型现象，因为最常见的规模经济是固定成本分摊。随着规模扩大，固定成本的百分比优势会逐渐降低。所以这类情况很常见。我们一听到有人说自己有飞轮效应（暗示网络经济），都会觉得好笑。真正的网络效应通常很少见。关键在于实质性影响，而非是否存在飞轮效应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was actually going to ask about that one because in software and social consumer products, network effects is always the pitch. Once we get big enough, we create this huge barrier. You mentioned just now you often find that's not actually true. It's rarely something that'll become a barrier. Is there anything else you find with network? And I know your power is called network economies, not network effect. I guess just to be clear, are these the same thing in your mind with different words?
turns.zh: 我正想问这个问题，因为在软件和社交消费品领域，网络效应总是被大肆宣传。一旦规模足够大，便能形成巨大壁垒。你刚才提到，发现这往往并非事实。网络效应很少能真正成为壁垒。还有其他关于网络效应的发现吗？我知道你所谓的权力叫做网络经济学，而非网络效应。我想明确一下，两者在你看来是同一事物的不同表述吗？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, kind of. I mean I have called it a type of power. So for me it's only those things which clear the significance barrier, hurdle rather that they're a large material. And so there are lots of things that I would say have network effects but not network economies.
turns.zh: 是的，某种程度上是的。对我来说，只有那些能突破意义门槛、跨越障碍的东西，才称得上是实质性的。所以有很多东西有网络效应，但没有网络经济学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, interesting. Wait, can you speak to that? So there is a difference between these terms, network economies?
turns.zh: 哦，有意思。等等，你能详细说明一下吗？所以这两个术语有区别？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah. So for me the difference is materiality is that whether the value benefit is large enough to engender a price delta significant enough to give you materially different margins into the future.
turns.zh: 是的。对我来说，区别在于实质性影响——即价值带来的好处是否足够大，能产生足以产生显著价格差异、从而为未来带来显著利润差异的效果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, does that network effect have an actual impact on your business and your ability to price?
turns.zh: 基本上，网络效应对你的业务和定价能力是否真的有影响？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, it's not an impact, it's a material impact. So it could have... If it's a penny to your bottom line, that's one thing if it's a billion dollars or something else.
turns.zh: 是的，这不是一般的影响，而是实质性的影响。所以如果这只对你的利润带来一分钱的影响，那是一回事；但如果能带来十亿美元甚至更多，那就是另一回事了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's actually really interesting. Is there an example of a company that comes to mind, they had network effects but not network economies as a power?
turns.zh: 哇，这真的很有趣。能否举个例子，说明有哪家公司拥有网络效应，但不具备网络经济优势？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: I think you could turn almost anywhere and get some modest network effects and any platform business would probably likely have some modest network effects. You asked me earlier and you sent me about Uber and Lyft, I'd say that they probably have network effects involved but not network economies.
turns.zh: 我觉得几乎任何领域都能找到一些温和的网络效应，任何平台型企业可能都会有一些温和的网络效应。你之前问过我，我给你发了优步和Lyft的案例。我觉得它们可能确实有网络效应，但没有网络经济优势。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's interesting. And the reason you're saying they don't have network economies is because they're still so competitive they still have to spend so much money to stay ahead and so the network is not-
turns.zh: 哇，这很有意思。你说它们没有网络经济优势的原因是，它们竞争太激烈了，不得不花费大量资金保持领先，所以网络效应——

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah. Right. The advantage that they get, it's not material. Right.
turns.zh: 对。没错。它们获得的优势并不显著。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that's so interesting. Along those lines, it's so interesting to see Uber and Lyft these days. In theory they both had some sort of strong network effect. I was just looking, so Lyft is 5% the market cap of Uber. Is there a lesson from just what it is that allowed Uber to just win and kind of run away with the market essentially?
turns.zh: 哇，这太有意思了。说到这点，看看优步和Lyft这两家公司很有意思。理论上，它们都拥有强大的网络效应。我刚查了一下，Lyft的市值只有优步的5%。这里有什么教训吗？是什么让优步最终胜出并基本占据了市场？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: I'm not entirely sure, I'll take a guess, but take it as a unformed guess. I haven't really studied it carefully. I think that over time there, if I had to guess, I'd say they're probably modest scale economies in the business. And over time Uber has just very successfully played a war of attrition. And that's both been in how they run their... They made one initial misstep, which is they misdefined their business. They said it was international transportation and it's not. That business is extremely geographically specific. (00:28:14): If you have a great position in the Bay Area, it doesn't help you in London. And so their forays into China and everything really didn't make, but they pulled back on that, focused down on understanding their source of power, which was a geographically specific scale economy. And then they've done interesting things like Uber Eats where they've tried to utilize the platform that they have to get other opportunities for the one side of their platform, the drivers. And so if I had to guess, I'd say it was a well-played war of attrition with modest scale economies.
turns.zh: 我不太确定，我只能猜猜，但这只是个不成熟的猜测。我没有仔细研究过。我认为随着时间推移，如果让我猜的话，我会说它们在业务中可能有温和的规模经济。优步通过了一场消耗战，最终胜出。首先，他们犯了一个初始错误，把业务定义错了。他们说这是国际运输，但实际上不是。这项业务对地理位置的依赖性极强。如果你在湾区占据有利位置，但在伦敦却毫无用处。所以他们进军中国市场等尝试并不成功，但后来他们撤退了，专注于理解自己的核心优势——地理特定的规模经济。然后他们还做了有趣的事情，比如Uber Eats，试图利用现有平台为司机一方创造其他机会。所以如果让我猜的话，我会说这是一场打得很巧妙的消耗战，伴随着温和的规模经济。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is that attrition coming from a source of power or is that just like a broader, more strict?
turns.zh: 这种消耗战是来自某种核心优势，还是更广泛、更严格的竞争？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, it only works because there are modest scale economies. If there weren't any then if they did all this stuff, they'd still have a global and see.
turns.zh: 是的，这只因为有温和的规模经济才行得通。如果没有规模经济，即便他们做了所有这些努力，最终还是会面临全球性的竞争。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Let me go in a slightly different direction. We've talked about power, we've talked about strategy. There's also, there's this word moat that comes up a lot. Everyone's always trying to build a moat. In your mind, is a moat equivalent to a power? Is there a difference when people talk about these two?
turns.zh: 明白了。让我换个方向讨论。我们谈到了核心优势，也谈到了战略。还有个词叫“护城河”，经常被提及。每个人都在努力构建护城河。在你看来，护城河和核心优势是一回事吗？在谈论这两个概念时，两者有区别吗？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Power requires a benefit and a barrier, you have to have something that you do that gives you a better outcome than your competitors, lower cost or higher price, and then something that makes it impossible for somebody else to mimic that. So moat is the second. So it's not synonymous with power because you can have a moat around a very undesirable piece of property and wouldn't get you far. But I think it is pretty synonymous with barrier. I think Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, I admire enormously. I think I get credit for popularizing those concepts and I think the way they think about it is good. I'd say that 7 Powers is probably more systematic and comprehensive in saying that. I don't think. This is wonderful. I don't know if you've read any of the Microsoft antitrust literature that came out of their-
turns.zh: 权力需要具备两个条件：一是获得某种优势，二是设置难以模仿的壁垒。也就是说，你必须做一些能带来比竞争对手更优结果的事——无论是降低成本还是提高价格——同时还要确保其他人无法复制这些优势。因此，护城河（moat）是第二个要素。它与权力并非完全等同，因为你可以在一块毫无价值的地产周围建起护城河，但这并不能让你走得太远。不过我认为它与壁垒（barrier）的概念非常相似。我非常敬仰沃伦·巴菲特和查理·芒格。我觉得自己在推广这些理念方面有所贡献，他们的思考方式也很有价值。我认为《七种权力》（7 Powers）在系统性和全面性上更胜一筹。不过我不确定——这太棒了。你读过微软反垄断案的相关文献吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: ...lawsuit, but there was a communication between Bill Gates and Warren Buffett where Warren Buffett was saying why he couldn't invest in Microsoft. He just didn't understand it. And so that meant the idea of network economies and what the moat was there he didn't understand. But I think the concept of a moat is a good one. The idea that you have something that gives you a refuge from competing forces.
turns.zh: ……那场诉讼期间，比尔·盖茨和沃伦·巴菲特有过一次交流。沃伦·巴菲特解释为何不投资微软，称自己不理解网络经济和护城河的概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of Warren Buffett, I found the quote about moats. Warren Buffett famously said, "In business, I look for economic castles protected by unreachable moats."
turns.zh: 关于沃伦·巴菲特，我记得他提到护城河的名言：“在商业中，我寻找的是被不可逾越的护城河保护的经济城堡。”

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Right. And so he's taking care of the benefit part by saying a castle.
turns.zh: 没错。他把利益部分处理得很到位，比作城堡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. He's got it covered.
turns.zh: 对。他把这部分考虑得很周到。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: But one of the tricks to understanding power is you have to have a pretty good understanding of why it's a castle and not a shack. So I'll give you a Netflix example. So a company I admire a lot, and I think if some of the things that they had to do to develop their business were so important for their business that don't guarantee a castle. So for example, UI development, it's been an enormous amount of resources on trying to get just the very best UI, I mean a zillion AB tests, all kinds of things. Their recommendation engine, everybody's knows the story about how that went, their interface with the content world and all this. So those things are important. They're things they have to spend a lot of time and resources on, but they can largely be mimicked. (00:32:31): So when Netflix in an earlier phase was fighting Blockbuster, when Blockbuster finally threw in the towel, said, "Well, we done. Well, better do a mail or a DVD business." If you look at the Blockbuster site, their UI site, you couldn't tell it different from Netflix. They just copied it. And so all that thoughtfulness about which things you put first and how you structure it and all that to make this suitable was mimicable. So that's an understanding of looking at the properties you have and trying to figure out if they're a castle or a shack.
turns.zh: 但理解权力的关键在于，你得清楚为什么它是城堡而非棚屋。以Netflix为例。我非常钦佩这家公司，我认为他们为发展业务必须做的一些事对其成功至关重要，但这些努力并不足以构建护城河。比如用户界面开发，他们投入了大量资源打造极致的UI，进行了无数次A/B测试。他们的推荐引擎，众所周知那段历史……与内容世界的对接等等。这些都是重要的工作，他们投入了大量时间和资源，但这些努力都容易被模仿。（00:32:31）：早期Netflix与百视达（Blockbuster）竞争时，当百视达最终认输、转向邮寄或DVD业务时，你会发现百视达的UI网站与Netflix几乎无异。他们直接抄袭了后者。因此，仔细思考哪些要素是优先级最高的，如何进行架构设计，这些努力才能真正形成护城河，而非简易的棚屋。

turns.en: I love that. This episode is brought to you by Paragon, the embedded integration platform for B2B SaaS product development teams. Visit useparagon.com/Lenny to see how Paragon can help you go to market faster with integrations today. That's use paragon.com/Lenny. So let's take this concept of 7 Powers. turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。本期节目由Paragon赞助播出——Paragon是面向B2B SaaS产品开发团队的嵌入式集成平台。你的用户是否经常要求与他们使用的其他SaaS平台进行新集成？遗憾的是，原生产品集成需要数月工程开发时间，且维护工作永无止境。Paragon通过消除认证复杂性、混乱的第三方API及集成错误调试等难题，让你的工程团队集成速度比内部开发快7倍。CopyAI、Cinch、TLDB等100多家SaaS公司的工程团队都在使用Paragon，这样他们就能专注于核心产品功能而非集成工作。（00:33:53）：最终成果是按需快速完成集成，进而提升产品使用率、增强用户留存率并促进客户追加消费。访问useparagon.com/Lenny，了解Paragon如何助力你加速集成上市。网址是useparagon.com/Lenny。接下来谈谈7大核心能力。我们很多听众都是新产品开发团队的个人贡献者产品经理，或者正在迭代现有产品。面对这些关于如何构建优势与障碍的知识，你建议他们如何应用？比如我正在开发新产品，你有什么建议？他们本周或下个月能做些什么，将这些经验融入到正在开发的产品中？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: I'd say they're a few and it's a little bit different. I'm not a great fan of the strategically driven organization because that idea, because it fuzzes over how this knowledge is useful at different stages in the business. And so for somebody in that position, say a product manager in an existing successful business. So it is important in terms of just understanding their business to know what their source of power is because they... And that can inform them about what it is that they're working for. And also they may see things since they're down in the weeds, they may see things that are important to that that they need to bring to other people's attention. Because they're the ones that really have the knowledge of what the heck's going on. There's another aspect I mentioned before, this idea of transforming, of starting up entirely new things. And usually... I wouldn't say, usually I say it's not uncommon for ideas about that to bubble up from down below. (00:36:03): And so that's another source. So let's separate a business into three phases, origination, takeoff, and stability. So the answers I've given are more in the stability phase. In the takeoff phase, let's say you've launched a product, you've gotten customer traction, now you're in a phase where there's just very rapid growth, probably other entrants like you, what are you facing? What you're facing is remember that underneath all of this is a change in technology. That's what made the product market fit possible in the first place. But that doesn't just stop. That if you're in a technology wave, often there are all kinds of offshoots both for you and the compliments to your business and everything else going on at the same time. (00:36:59): And to win at that stability phase, which is really a market share win, you have to be aware of those and understand, okay, we have to incorporate this new feature. Or maybe now things have gotten to the point where this new market segment is, our product is attractive before it wasn't. This is meat and potato stuff for somebody at that level and it may well be the decisive element in terms of whether you win that market share battle with the other contenders. And so you have a very, very important role at that point. And so I'd say the first thing to do with your question is to make sure you think about the different phases of this and then ask what those responsibilities are.
turns.zh:
我得说这种情况并不多见，而且各有不同。我不太喜欢那种战略驱动型组织，因为这种理念会模糊知识在不同业务阶段的实用性。对于身处现有成功企业的产品经理等职位的人而言，了解自身的核心竞争力至关重要，因为这能让他们明确奋斗目标。同时，由于身处一线，他们能洞察到关键问题，并将这些见解传递给其他团队——毕竟他们才是真正掌握业务脉络的人。

我之前提到的另一个关键点是，创新型变革与全新事业的开创往往源自基层的智慧火花。（00:36:03）因此，我们可以将企业发展分为三个阶段：创立期、起飞期和稳定期。我给出的答案更多聚焦于稳定期。在起飞期，产品成功推出，获得客户认可后，企业将迎来快速增长阶段，可能面临竞争对手的挑战。此时，核心问题在于技术变革的驱动。技术浪潮往往催生出多样化的分支机遇，这既为自身创造机遇，也为竞争对手提供新思路。

（00:36:59）要在稳定期赢得市场份额，关键在于敏锐捕捉这些机遇。比如，某个新兴市场细分领域可能使产品更具吸引力。这对高层而言是常识性的洞察，却可能是决定市场份额争夺成败的关键因素。因此，稳定期需要高管具备战略把控能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about for people that are just trying to get better at being strategic, thinking strategically something every product leader is always encouraged to do, become a better strategic thinker, build as muscle of strategy, what do you often advise to people just get better at the stuff? Obviously read your book.
turns.zh: 对于那些希望提升战略思维能力的人——毕竟每个产品负责人都被鼓励成为战略型人才——你通常会给出什么建议？显然，阅读你的书籍是关键。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Read the book, and then have conversations with your colleagues about the topic because as you internalize what that means and how, have conversations with them about do we really have this kind of power? What's going on here? What's important? What isn't. Those conversations tend to allow you to get a better grip on things. I mean in the case of Netflix, Reed actually had me come in and train the top a hundred people in Netflix and strategy. We actually ran classes in the company, but that's unusual I'd say. And I didn't have the book yet. And so I think the book gets people pretty far down that path already.
turns.zh: 阅读书籍后，与同事探讨相关话题至关重要。当你深入理解其核心含义与实践方法时，与他们交流：我们是否真的拥有这种影响力？当前局势的核心是什么？哪些因素至关重要？哪些则无关紧要。这种对话能帮助你更清晰地把握全局。以Netflix为例，里德曾邀请我为其百名高管讲授战略课程。我们在公司内部开展了培训，但这种案例实属罕见。当时我尚未完成书稿，所以我认为这本书已经为读者指明了清晰的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you don't do that anymore, I imagine if someone wanted to do that today, not an option.
turns.zh: 如今你不再做这些事了。我觉得如果有人想在今天重操旧业，那根本行不通。

And so I don't. I enjoyed that immensely wonderful people to work with. But sadly I don't have the time.
turns.zh: 很遗憾，我现在没有时间了。我的意思是，我确实经常在公司会议上参加座谈会之类的活动，但不会开设完整的课程了，而且我也不再在斯坦福大学任教了。所以我现在没法做这些了。我很享受那段时光，与优秀的人共事真是太棒了。但可惜我现在没有时间了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're about to get a lot of requests for fireside chats. I hope you're ready. You mentioned AI at some point in our chat. I'm curious how you think AI is going to change your 7 Powers framework. Do you think defensibility goes down in general? Will certain forms of power become more important or harder to achieve? How do you think about AI?
turns.zh: 你很快会收到很多参加座谈会的邀请。希望你能做好准备。在我们的聊天中，你提到了人工智能。我很好奇你认为人工智能会如何改变你的“7大权力”框架。你觉得防御能力总体会下降吗？某些形式的权力会变得更重要或者更难获得吗？你对人工智能有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. I mean we're all in this phase of wondering exactly how generative AI is going to play out. My own view, currently I don't see any change in seven powers from it in terms of an eighth power or something. But the issues that it brings up, like scale economies, I mean think of scale economies. If you have a fixed cost of trying to develop a model of a billion dollars or something or network effects, will AI models develop so that they learn in a way that for one user's interaction helps another user's interaction? That would be a powerful network economy. Or if it learns, if you think of if it learns about you and becomes a better psychiatrist or something, then that's a switching cost. So all these things are relevant to which business models will work and I find that useful. (00:40:51): But I think in general, the way I think about it is it's a standard form of potentially very powerful technology that is being introduced into the business world and just asking how that plays out. I currently tend to think of that there's three types of plays. There's the company that's the technology play itself. So if you think of microprocessors, it would be Intel. There's the companies that wouldn't exist without the technology. So for semiconductors it would be Microsoft. And then there are the companies that utilize the technology, but it had existed before and after. So for semiconductors it would be automobiles. They used a ton of chips, but there were still cars before, after. (00:41:48): And so I'm of the view, I'm very much uncertain at this point that generative AI, its biggest impact will be that tertiary class. It will be used in a lot of things that existed before and exist after, but are made better by it like semiconductors and automobiles. And so it reminds me, if you think of really big technology shifts like this, it reminds me of electricity. When electricity came, you could completely reconfigure a factory floor. You no longer had to have... You could have the power source essentially at the operating unit of an operator. But that took a lot of redesign, incorporation, investment, learning, complements, all kinds of stuff. I tend to think this will be more like that. There will be some pure cases. People will want to have them write their term paper with ChatGPT or something. But if you think of businesses, it's hard for me to think of a single functional area in a business that with redesign couldn't benefit. So accounting, HR, R&D all have uses of this but requires incorporation, which is always troublesome. (00:43:30): And so that's my view. But there certainly will be businesses that couldn't exist without it. And there's some that are coming up and some of those are in fact the businesses that empower the tertiary need, they're the ones that bring in. But if you go back, this will date me, but if you go back into business history, back in, I guess it was the 90s, there was this thing called business process re-engineering, the idea that you could take a computer sensibility into business processes, redesign them and get these monstrous cost savings. And it was a gigantic consulting opportunity for people. Whole companies got developed based on that and it feels more like that to me, but it's very interesting. I could be wrong, but it feels different than crypto. It feels like there's more of a real ultimate use case. I mean, if it really is true what they say that a 50% improvement in programming efficacy is not uncommon, just that proposition alone is worth an awful lot of money if you think how many programmers are in the world.
turns.zh:
是的，这确实是个很棒的问题。我想我们现在都处在一个阶段，试图弄清楚生成式人工智能将如何发展。我个人的看法是，目前我认为它对现有七大巨头（如谷歌、亚马逊、Facebook等）不会产生任何根本性影响。但它引发的诸多问题，比如规模经济——比如说，你想想规模经济。如果开发一个价值十亿美元的模型需要固定成本，或者网络效应会如何发挥？当AI模型能够通过一个用户的交互帮助另一个用户时，那将是强大的网络经济效应。又或者如果AI能通过学习了解你，成为更好的心理医生，那就是转换成本。所以所有这些问题都与哪些商业模式能成功息息相关，我觉得这很有价值。  

（00:40:51）：但总的来说，我的看法是，这是一项潜力巨大的标准技术，正被引入商业世界，我们只需观察其发展路径。目前我倾向于认为有三种应用模式。第一种是技术本身的应用公司。比如微处理器领域的英特尔。第二种是因技术而诞生的公司，比如半导体领域的微软。第三种是利用技术的公司，但技术在此前和此后都存在，比如汽车行业。汽车使用大量芯片，但无论技术如何变化，汽车始终存在。  

（00:41:48）：所以我的观点是，目前我对生成式人工智能的最大影响持谨慎态度，它将应用于许多既有领域，但通过技术提升其质量，比如半导体和汽车。这让我联想到重大技术变革，比如电力革命。当电力出现时，工厂可以彻底改造，不再需要集中供电，而是将电源置于操作单元附近。但这需要大量重新设计、整合、投资、学习和配套设施等。生成式人工智能的情况可能类似。当然会有纯粹的应用场景，比如用ChatGPT写论文。但就商业领域而言，我很难想到有哪个职能部门不受益于重新设计。比如会计、人力资源、研发等领域都有应用空间，但整合始终是个难题。  

（00:43:30）：以上就是我的看法。但肯定会有因技术而诞生的公司。有些新兴公司实际上正满足第三类需求，带来技术红利。但回顾历史，这让我暴露年龄——上世纪90年代，商业流程再造思潮兴起，主张将计算机思维融入业务流程，重构流程以实现巨额成本节约。这曾为咨询公司创造巨大商机，甚至有公司因此诞生。生成式人工智能给我的感觉更类似，但更有趣。我可能错了，但它与加密货币不同，感觉有更真实的终极应用场景。比如如果真如所言，编程效率提升50%并非异想天开，单这一点就价值巨大。
全球有多少程序员？

turns.en: No question. You mentioned eighth power. I just want to check, is there an emerging eighth power you wish you maybe would've included or maybe added in the future that's like, "Oh, maybe this is on the edge," or it's like, "Nope, we got these seven?"
turns.zh: 没问题啊。你提到第八大势力。我想确认一下，是否有新兴的第八大势力你希望能纳入或在未来加入？比如“哦，或许这算个边缘势力”，或者“不行，我们就认定这七个了”？

turns.en: It's a great question. I'm always looking for it because if you find it it probably means it's so obscure there, it'll also be a great investment opportunity. We're looking all the time, but so far, no. So far I'm pretty satisfied that seven is an exhaustive set, but never say never. That's an empirical seven, not a theoretical seven.
turns.zh: 这是个很棒的问题。我一直在寻找这样的势力，因为如果能找到它，可能意味着它在某个领域非常冷门，也会是一个绝佳的投资机会。我们一直在寻找，但目前还没有。到目前为止，我对七个势力的完整性还是比较满意的，但永远不要说永远不行。这些是经验总结出的七个势力，而不是理论上的七个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If we start seeing you making incredible returns, you've clearly found an eighth power [inaudible 00:45:41]-
turns.zh: 如果我们开始看到你获得惊人的回报，那显然你找到了第八大势力[00:45:41语音不清]-

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to close one thread on a power that you mentioned that is often a pitfall, which is around process power and basically execution. A lot of people think so in a lot of decks it's like, oh, we have the most amazing team, we move the fastest, we're earliest. You mentioned how rarely is that actually a power actually being able to execute and create a process that is an actual barrier? Can you just talk a bit more about that to help people understand okay, it's probably not our power?
turns.zh: 我想最后再讨论一个你提到的、常成为陷阱的势力——流程能力和执行力。很多人在很多商业计划书中都认为，“我们有最棒的团队，行动最迅速，抢占先机”。你提到过，很少有企业真正能把执行力转化为优势，建立流程才是真正的壁垒。能否再详细谈谈，帮助大家理解或许这根本不是我们的优势？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: One of the great thinkers in strategy was this Harvard professor Michael Porter, and he in probably 40 years ago, made the very controversial statement that operational excellence is not strategy. He got a lot of people of the Harvard Business School faculty really mad at him because that's what their careers were about and it sounded like he was dissing them. But the point he was making was when you get to this end state, if you already have power that things that drive operational excellence can be mimicked because you can hire a consulting firm who has best practices, knowledges that come in and get you up to snuff. You can hire people from your competitors who know how to do it better. And that's true, but it's also true in this takeoff phase in a business that we talked about before, when you're trying to attain competitive position, operational excellence is everything. (00:47:14): And so if you think of strategy, not statically endpoints like Professor Porter was, but if you look at dynamically how you get there, operational excellence is essential for a strategy. So think of those things I mentioned before about Netflix, about their UI and recommendation engine and so on, or international rollout, all those things. They were in a battle to get more subscribers than other people and those were critical for that. But in themselves, they're critical in attaining competitive position, but in themselves, they're not sources of power typically, unless there's some very tight considerations here or very demanding considerations for the... Unless if they have to be material, but they also have to be opaque or some way people can't easily imitate them. Either they don't understand what's going on or they might be opaque. So for example, think of TSMC. So when they put up the latest fab and get that operational, are there a lot of steps in doing that? (00:48:43): They know how to do with their staff is trained to do it, but it's not documented necessarily and you can't imitate it. Then maybe they have it. I don't know if they have process power or not, but it takes that level of complexity. In my book, I use the example of Toyota and a car manufacturing is complex enough that you can have this opacity in terms of material steps, but it's not common. So if you're in a stability phase of business, you're stuck with this funny thing, which is most of your day is on those issues and it should be because if you don't do it, a competitor can and they can end up better than you. And so you're on a treadmill and that's the way business is. That's fine. And if you stop running that treadmill, you get creamed. So you got to do it, it's most of your day, but it's not power. And there are those rare cases where it's so material and so inimitable that it can be power, but they're rare.
turns.zh:
哈佛商学院教授迈克尔·波特（Michael Porter）是战略领域的杰出思想家之一。大约40年前，他提出了一个极具争议的观点：运营卓越并非战略所在。这番言论让哈佛商学院的许多教师大为光火，因为这关乎他们的职业生涯，波特仿佛在贬低他们。但他的核心观点是，当企业达到稳定阶段，已然拥有竞争优势时，模仿运营卓越的手段就变得轻而易举——你可以聘请拥有最佳实践的咨询公司，引入专业知识迅速提升；也可以从竞争对手那里挖来更擅长此道的人才。这种说法固然有理，但在我们之前讨论的业务起飞阶段，追求竞争地位时，运营卓越才是关键所在。

（00:47:14）因此，若不将战略视为波特教授所说的静态终点，而是动态地审视达成目标的过程，运营卓越便成为战略的核心要素。以Netflix为例，其用户界面、推荐引擎等核心技术，或国际化扩张策略，都曾助力争夺订阅用户，这类创新对竞争地位至关重要，但本身并非竞争优势的源泉，除非存在极其严格的考量标准。例如，台积电（TSMC）在新建晶圆厂时，虽然员工经过专业培训，但流程未必成文，难以被模仿。这种不透明性或许源于技术复杂性，也可能是对手难以理解的技术壁垒。

（00:48:43）在我的著作中，我以丰田为例，汽车制造业的复杂性足以形成材料步骤上的不透明性，但这种情况实属罕见。当企业处于稳定阶段时，日常工作多围绕这些问题打转，停滞不前就会被竞争对手超越。这是商业的常态。若停下脚步，必将被淘汰。因此，尽管这些工作占据了大部分时间，却并非战略核心。只有在少数情况下，核心流程极具关键性且不可模仿时，才能转化为战略优势，但这种情况实属罕见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like the heuristic that if you haven't written it down or you can't describe it, that might be a sign that maybe process power is a power of yours.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个启发性观点：如果你无法将其书面化或描述出来，或许这正是流程权力成为你核心竞争力的信号。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah. And there isn't a consulting firm that offers to bring you up to speed on that.
turns.zh: 是的。而且没有咨询公司能提供快速提升的服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They'll make you more like Amazon as a service. Kind of along these same lines, you talk about how the only things that create value in a company are power, market size and operational excellence. And I think hearing that will blow a lot of people's minds because they think there's so many things that contribute to the value of a company and you whittle it down to these three things. What can you say about that insight?
turns.zh: 他们会让你们的服务更像亚马逊。说到这点，你们提到在一家公司中创造价值的唯一因素是权力、市场规模和卓越运营。我觉得很多人听到这话会感到震惊，因为他们认为有太多因素能为公司增值，而你们却把它归结为这三个要素。对此你有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: So I'd say they're right and I'm right. They're right because there are this incredible... I mean business is really hard and there are just a multitude of things you have to pay attention for. I'm right because all those things fall into those three categories. So it's an exhaustive set and it simply comes out of the math. So we're both right I'd say.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得他们说得对，我也说得对。他们说得对是因为商业环境确实极其复杂，有太多需要关注的方面。我说得对是因为所有这些因素都能归入这三个类别。这是一个详尽的集合，完全是从数学逻辑推导出来的。所以我觉得我们俩都没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, the intent of a lot of your work is to empower founders. I'm curious if you've noticed any broad economic trends or shifts that you think will make life easier or harder for founders in the coming years?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你大部分工作的核心目标是赋能创始人。我很好奇，你是否注意到任何宏观经济趋势或变化，你认为这些变化会在未来几年让创始人的创业之路更顺畅还是更艰难？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Personally, I am very, very concerned about the debt trajectory of the United States and of many countries around the world, but I'll pick on the United States, but it's a trend going on everywhere. We're on a trajectory for this extremely high indebtedness. And so if you think about the last 30 years, right? There's been a crisis about once every 10 years. So there's the dot-com bust, there's the financial crisis, there was COVID. Nothing makes me think that the frequency will be a lot less. I don't know what, who knows? These are all uncertain events. But imagine if we got to one of those and we had no dry powder and dry powder for us is the ability to heavily deficit spend take on debt. And fortunately our government did that in both the financial crisis and in COVID. And because that people had jobs. My own view about the financial crisis is that if we hadn't done that, plus having Ben Bernanke as the head of the Fed, we would've gone into another great depression. (00:52:52): It was that ugly. So this current debt trajectory, you don't know how long it will take exactly when, but eventually that will mean we will not have dry powder. People will not respect the credit worthiness of this country. So that worries me a lot. And it utterly will affect the idea of company founding because if you get into a crisis like that, the capital markets lock up and it gets very difficult to do anything. And to really stretch my credibility here, I'll opine on just how hard a problem this is to solve. The reason this is so difficult for this country to solve and other countries is that it is right at the crux of the delicate dance between capitalism and democracy. So if you think about the problem, of course that's driving all this is entitlements. There's discretionary spending, certain recovery programs and stuff, but those can go away. The underlying trend that people just can't get their arms around is entitlements. And anybody who looks at the numbers can see that. Every economist knows that. But that's not an easy fix. (00:54:18): And the reason it's not an easy fix is there are two opposing views of what's going on, and there's no way to resolve those two views. One is that capitalism is rapacious and results in more and more inequality and the government has to do something about it. And the other is that the government is on a path that is creeping socialism that will undermine our freedom and economic sufficiency. And the poster child for the rapacious capitalism. One is, I don't know if you've seen the recent analysis of inequality in the United States just came out, much more robust analysis. And it said that basically inequality in the last 60 years of the United States is unchanged, but that's post-transfer, post-tax inequality, which basically says the amount of taxing and transferring going on was about right. So it says that the amount we're spending is about right from that perspective, that it compensates for the other inequities and we should be spending that much so we should tax more. (00:55:30): And the poster child for the other point of view of the dangers of government is the steadily increasing without interruption percentage of the economy that is government. And to levels that 75 years ago, people would've thought absolutely impossible. So there are these two views about what's going on. One is that we're compensating for the normal inequities of capitalism, and the other is that we're headed down a path to socialism and ruin. And that leads to a deadlock, which is you don't tax anymore and you don't cut spending and that leaves deficits. So anyway, a long, long rant, sorry but that trend is extremely politically difficult to deal with and extremely threatening and that concerns me immensely.
turns.zh:
就我个人而言，我对美国以及全球许多国家的债务增长趋势深感担忧，但我要特别指出美国的情况。不过这其实是全球普遍趋势。我们正朝着极高债务水平的方向发展。如果回顾过去30年，大约每10年就会爆发一次危机——先是互联网泡沫破裂，接着是金融危机，再到新冠疫情。没有任何迹象表明这种频率会降低。我不知道未来会怎样，谁又能预料呢？这些都是不确定性事件。但想象一下，如果我们遭遇下一次危机，却没有足够的财政缓冲——所谓“干粉”（dry powder）指的是通过赤字支出和举债来应对危机的能力——幸运的是，我们的政府在金融危机和新冠疫情期间都采取了这种措施，保住了就业岗位。我对金融危机的看法是，如果当时没有采取这些措施，再加上贝南克（Ben Bernanke）担任美联储主席，我们很可能陷入另一场大萧条。（00:52:52）当时的形势极其严峻。就当前债务增长趋势而言，虽然无法准确预测何时触发危机，但最终必然导致我们失去财政缓冲，国际社会将不再信任美国的信用评级。这让我深感担忧。这种情况将直接影响创业环境，因为一旦陷入危机局面，资本市场就会陷入停滞，各种行动都将举步维艰。为了充分说明这个问题的复杂性，我要指出其核心难点在于资本主义与民主制度之间的微妙平衡。问题的根源在于福利支出——比如离散性支出、某些经济复苏计划等——但这些政策终将退场，而真正无法解决的深层问题是福利制度。任何分析人士都能看清这一点，每位经济学家都心知肚明，但这绝非易事。

（00:54:18）难点在于两种截然相反的观点无法调和。一派认为资本主义是无情的，会导致日益加剧的不平等，政府必须采取措施纠正；另一派则认为政府正滑向社会主义道路，侵蚀自由与经济活力。关于资本主义贪婪性的典型例子是美国近期发布的收入不平等研究报告，该研究指出过去60年美国不平等程度基本未变，但这是扣除税收和转移支付后的数据，意味着税收与转移支付规模合理，足以抵消其他不公，政府支出规模应维持现状。另一方面，政府占经济比重持续攀升，达到75年前难以想象的水平。这两种观点陷入僵局：一派主张弥补资本主义固有不平等，另一派则警告走向社会主义与经济崩溃。
这样一来，就产生了财政赤字。总之，我说了好多，抱歉，但这种趋势在政治上极难应对，极具威胁性，这让我深感担忧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Not to leave listeners with a very sad state of affairs.
turns.zh: 以免让听众陷入一种非常沮丧的境地。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, sorry.
turns.zh: 对不起啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, no. I think this is important. I think it's important people think about this and know these things. Is there anything that gives you hope? Is there anything that gets you excited about either for founders or anyone in general, just to leave folks with maybe on a happy?
turns.zh: 不，不。我觉得这很重要。我认为让人们思考这些问题、了解这些知识很重要。有什么能给你们带来希望的事吗？有什么能让创始人或者普通人兴奋起来的事吗？就是想让大家离开时能感受到一丝快乐。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I am an optimist really in a way, and I do. There's a famous Austrian and eventually American economist named Joseph Schumpeter who wrote this wonderful book Theory of Economic Development way back when over a hundred years ago, where he took the unusual view of saying that the vitality of an economy depended on entrepreneurs. And I ascribe to that. I think that creativity and action are the ways society and people advance. And I think the US's and a free society has huge advantages in that. And I think that I feel very lucky to be in a place I'm in Silicon Valley, but to be in a place in a country where that is vital and active and I think that's ground zero for me. And so I think you see that alive and well, I think. And there are people that are very Enthusiastic about that as I am.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得自己在某种程度上是个乐观主义者。我确实这么认为。有位著名的奥地利经济学家、后来成为美国经济学家的约瑟夫·熊彼特，早在一百多年前就写了一本精彩的著作《经济发展理论》。他提出了一个不同寻常的观点，即经济的活力取决于企业家。我认同这一观点。我认为创造力和行动是社会和人类进步的方式。我认为美国和自由社会在这方面具有巨大优势。我觉得自己很幸运能身处硅谷这样的地方，身处一个充满活力和生机的地方，对我来说这里就是原点。我觉得你能感受到这种活力，我相信和我一样对此充满热情的人也很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful way to close out our chat. Is there anything else you want to share before we get to our very exciting lightning round? Is there anything you want to leave listeners with or any last tidbit of advice?
turns.zh: 以这样的方式结束我们的对话真是太好了。在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的吗？有什么想留给听众的或者最后的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: I alluded to it before, but just that remember, action is the first principle of business. You do stuff and my book is very oriented towards that. The idea was not to tell you what to do, but to give you guideposts while you're on that journey. People that are enthused about it, I encourage you to do stuff. That's where it all starts and I can think about it and maybe help a little bit, but it's mostly doing stuff.
turns.zh: 我之前提过，但还是要提醒大家，行动是商业的第一原则。你去行动，我的书就是围绕这一点展开的。我的初衷不是告诉你该做什么，而是为你的行动之旅提供指引。对于那些对此充满热情的人，我鼓励你们去行动。这就是一切的起点，我可以思考一下，或许能提供一些帮助，但最重要的是去行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that point so much. It was something I was going to touch on but I didn't get to is just there's so many people that just sit around and theorize about a strategy of their business, especially in their early stage. Here's our grand master plan, here's an amazing strategy or just read about startup ideas and don't actually try it. I love this final note of just try it. Just do it. Don't just sit there and-
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个观点了。这是我本想提到的但没来得及说的，就是太多人只是坐着理论化他们的商业策略，尤其是在创业初期。我们的宏伟计划是这个，绝妙的策略是那个，或者只是读读创业想法，却从不付诸实践。我太喜欢最后这个“去行动吧”的观点了。去行动吧。生活充满惊喜。你最终会到达一个意想不到的地方。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, just do it. And life is full of surprises. You'll end up in a place you didn't expect.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，就去行动吧。生活充满惊喜，你最终会到达一个意想不到的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Speaking of ending up in a place you didn't expect, it's time for our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到到达一个意想不到的地方，是时候进入我们激动人心的闪电问答环节了。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Oh, sure. I'll do my best here. I'm not very good on lightning.
turns.zh: 哦，好的，我会尽力的。我不太擅长闪电问答。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，您向他人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: One book that is extremely wonky, and I can only take it in very small doses, but is magnificent, is one called The Road to Reality by Roger Penrose, who's this brilliant mathematician. And it will be very daunting for anybody unless you're a deep math person, but his brilliance in erudition just shines through in this thing. And it's an amazing book. I would say there's another book, boy, I wish I could remember the name. Maybe you can get the name of the author called Gene by this geneticist. And I think he's a Harvard Medical School professor that's about the history of genetics and he is an absolutely luminous writer. I mean, it puts me to shame. I'm embarrassed when I read it because I think how pedestrian my writing is and incredibly knowledgeable about the history of genetics and I think that's such an important topic. So those are two that I would recommend highly, fairly wonky, but I like them both.
turns.zh: 有一本书非常晦涩，我只能一点点地读下去，但它确实很棒。这本书叫《通往现实之路》，作者是罗杰·彭罗斯——一位才华横溢的数学家。对于不精通数学的人来说，它可能会让人望而生畏，但他在学术造诣方面的才华在这本书中展露无遗。这是一本令人惊叹的著作。我还想推荐另一本书，天哪，我真希望能记得作者的名字。或许你能帮我想起那位基因学家的名字。作者是哈佛医学院的教授，研究基因史的，他的文笔简直才华横溢。读他的作品时，我不禁自惭形秽。相比之下，我觉得自己的写作太平庸了。基因史是一个如此重要的课题，所以这两本书我都强烈推荐，虽然确实有些晦涩，但我都爱不释手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love them. The author, I just looked him up. Siddhartha Mukherjee.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这本书。我刚查了一下作者，叫悉达尔塔·穆克吉。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yes. Just amazing. You read it and you go, "How did he think of that phrasing?" I mean, it's just, he's amazing.
turns.zh: 是啊。他简直太棒了。读他的作品时，你会感叹：“他怎么能想出这样的表达方式？”他太令人惊叹了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: I'm a huge movie fan and have been all my life, and I'm particularly keen on animated films. But the movie that I've recently seen that I liked particularly it was American Fiction. I thought that was... It didn't make any of the easy choices in a movie and as a result was just incredibly interesting and thoughtful I thought.
turns.zh: 我一直是个电影迷，尤其痴迷动画片。但最近我看了一部特别喜欢的电影，叫《美国虚构》。我觉得它……它没有走寻常的套路，因此特别引人入胜、发人深省。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 最近有没有发现特别喜欢的新产品？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: In my office, just this last week, we actually put a Persian rug in our entry room, and this is what's called a Farahan Sarouk rug and it's 150 years old. And it had an effect in me that I didn't expect, which is it is a work of great beauty. And it was before, it was all hand-done before machines. You get all this wonderful variation of the actual icons in the rug and the different dye colors. And I find that every morning when I walk in, I go, "That's really beautiful," and it's uplifting and it shows you the importance of, or the value of the quality of art. I mean, just blows my mind actually. So that's probably not the usual product discussion that you get.
turns.zh: 就在上周，我们办公室在入口处铺了一块波斯地毯，叫法哈兰萨鲁克地毯，已有150年历史了。它对我的影响远超预期——它真是件极美的艺术品。这块地毯是在机器普及之前手工制作的，地毯上的图案和不同染料颜色都极具变化。每天早上走进办公室，我都会感叹：“真美啊！”它能振奋人心，也让我意识到艺术品质的重要性。这可不是常见的商品推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I love that answer. Recently we've had some really unique choices. One is a very nice Mercedes and a Rivian and a minivan recently. We've got a lot of very nice things.
turns.zh: 不，我喜欢你的回答。我们最近收到了一些非常独特的选择。比如一辆梅赛德斯、一辆Rivian，还有一辆小型货车。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Oh, that's great. I'm a car guy too, so I didn't answer on the car question.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。我也是个爱车人士，所以我没回答那个关于汽车的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, I love that. We have Rory Sutherland coming on the podcast soon. He is one of the leaders of Ogilvy and he has a whole thing about how buying a home is the best value of art to buy art if you live in a home that makes you feel inspired and is beautiful.
turns.zh: 天哪，我超爱这个话题。我们很快会邀请罗里·萨瑟兰上节目。他是奥美公司的领军人物，他有一番见解：如果你住在一个能激发灵感、充满美感的房子里，买房就是购买艺术品的最佳价值所在。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, I'm a big believer in that. I mean, I think that your place and how you connect to it has an important grounding effect. And then before I talked earlier about creativity and I think surrounding yourself in an environment that stimulates that is really important. And so I couldn't agree with him more.
turns.zh: 是的，我深信这一点。我觉得住所与你与它的连接有着重要的基础作用。此前我谈到过创造力，我认为身处能激发创造力的环境中真的很重要。所以我完全赞同他的观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often think about, come back to share with friends or family?
turns.zh: 还有两个问题。你有没有一个经常回想、喜欢与朋友或家人分享的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: One is what Clint Eastwood's advice to actors, which is don't just do something, stand there. And so there are a lot of things that are long-termish with low signal to noise. And you can often just do a lot of stuff that you think makes a difference, but it really doesn't. And so that's one. The other one which is somewhat more profound I think was one that I had a famous Sri Lankan journalist was a mentor of mine and very dear friend, and he had a favorite expression that I adhere to all the time, which is everything is always about something else.
turns.zh: 第一个是克林特·伊斯特伍德给演员的建议：别光做事，要学会等待。还有很多事情是长期主义的，但成效却微乎其微。你可能会做很多自以为能改变局面的事，但其实根本无济于事。这就是第一个。第二个更深刻一些——我有一位斯里兰卡著名的记者导师，他是我非常亲密的朋友。他有一句我一直奉行的格言：万事皆有深层含义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Deep.
turns.zh: 哇，真是深刻。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: And that's so true if you're dealing with this power stuff when if you really dig down, everything is always about something else.
turns.zh: 确实如此。如果你深入探讨权力问题，就会发现万事皆有深层含义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of power, final question. People that have a lot of power are leaders in the world. I'm curious, do you have a favorite historical leader?
turns.zh: 说到权力，最后一个问题。拥有巨大权力的人是世界领袖。我很好奇，你有没有特别欣赏的历史领袖？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: So yeah. I have some that I admire a great deal. I'm a tremendous fan of Winston Churchill's. Most really great people are quirky and he qualified. There are things you could say about him that you might not have liked that so much, but he was a genius and had great fortitude, human sense. He understood things long before other people. I've give him high marks. Some of the great artists I admire enormously. I'm reading a book right now on the last 20 years of Michelangelo, which wonderful book actually, and which is a very interesting period because in his first 70 years he finished up all that, he wasn't going to do sculpture anymore. He just finished The Last Judgment, which was the wall of the Sistine Chapel. (01:06:08): And I think the last major fresco he did. And a lot of his friends at that time, he was exiled from Florence and living in Rome and he had this Roman community and a lot of his close friends that had recently died or had difficulties. So he's at this inflection point in his life at 70, which in those days was very old, and yet he went on to do some of the most remarkable architecture in the history of the world. And so you've got to admire that. I mean, just doing that, which is that rare second act. But I think for world leaders, Winston Churchill is very high. I'm a fan of Teddy Roosevelt, I must say too, in this country.
turns.zh: 有啊。有几位我非常钦佩。我是温斯顿·丘吉尔的超级粉丝。大多数伟大人物都有些怪癖，他也不例外。关于他，有些你可能不喜欢的地方，但他是个天才，拥有非凡的勇气和人性。早在别人意识到之前，他就能洞察事物。我给他打高分。我还很欣赏一些伟大艺术家。我现在正在读一本关于米开朗基罗最后20年的书，写得非常棒。这段时期很特别，因为他前70年完成了所有作品，之后就不再雕塑了。他刚完成《最后的审判》——西斯廷教堂的壁画。（01:06:08）我认为这是他最后一幅重要壁画。当时他的许多朋友被流放到罗马，身边亲近的人不是离世就是遭遇困境。在70岁这个在当时已属高龄的年纪，他迎来人生转折点，却依然能创作出世界史上最非凡的建筑作品。这真令人敬佩。说到世界领袖，温斯顿·丘吉尔绝对名列前茅。在美国，我也很欣赏泰迪·罗斯福。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Hamilton, you are wonderful. I feel like we have helped a lot of people up-level their ability to think about strategy and moats and power. Thank you so much for being here. Two final questions. Where can folks find more online if they want to dig in further, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。汉密尔顿，你太棒了。我觉得我们帮助了很多人，提升了他们思考战略、护城河和权力的能力。这里要非常感谢你能来参加节目。最后两个问题。读者如果想深入了解，可以在哪里找到更多资料？听众又如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Yeah, so as I say, I'm an idea person and I'm about trying to empower company founders, and so only thing I can say is read the book, spread the ideas, start your own company. Those are the things that would make me happy.
turns.zh: 是的，正如我所说，我是个创意型人物，致力于赋能公司创始人。所以我能给出的唯一建议就是：读这本书，传播这些理念，创办自己的公司。这些事能让我感到快乐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Hamilton, Thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。汉密尔顿，非常感谢你能来参加节目。

turns.speaker: Hamilton Helmer
turns.en: Great. My pleasure, Lenny.
turns.zh: 不客气。乐意之至，莱尼。
